First you need to make sure your soil is right. pH, composition, organic matter. It's not as simple as sticking a few plants in some Miracle Gro planting soil friend. On average, building up a good fertile, friable soil that is pest and disease free takes roughly ten years. I do soil testing for the local university. I recommend getting a bunch of organics NOW and a good rototiller., or layer gardening alternating browns (leaves), greens (grass clippings) and a bunch of manure and hope it breaks down by spring. If you don't have the soil, not much is going to grow.

Lol, oh, we know... Trust me, we know :)

Our soil is pretty terrible, alkaline desert with low organic matter. We are close to an agriculture college so we have access to a lot of resources to test it and buy* the materials to improve it (*as long as the dollar holds out lol)

I think we've got a pretty decent plan of building it up in sections with lots of cover crops and green manures. I bought a flail mower and power harrow attachment for the tractor and for the first few years we are basically just going to be "growing good dirt" - we've got a handful of raised beds filled with a commercial compost mix, and a small assortment of hydroponics in the greenhouse to hold us over in the meantime.

The general plan on process has been: Clear it, level it, fence it, spread the chipped brush and compost on it, cover crop it, flail mow the cover crop, plant tillage radishes, crimp them down, let them rot, plant a cover crop, flail mow it, spread compost layer, go over it with the power harrow, plant cover crop, repeat....

We will see. A month ago we had a freak snow fall earlier than ever before recorded in our region and I looked out at the budding mini farm and said "I think I'm starting to understand exactly why farmers pray so much" but what is life if not an adventure?
